extracted.intended_audience: The Higher and Middle Classes (explicit addressee in the text)
extracted.subtask_description: A moral/political lay-sermon essay addressed to higher and middle classes arguing about the social effects of commerce, agriculture, and credit; mixes analytic argumentation with illustrative anecdotes and moral appeals. The page models rhetorical techniques for persuasive public prose of the 19th-century essay/sermon genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce facts as symptoms of a general state
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fact ie introduced not for ita own sake, but as symptom of the general state of men's feelings, as an evidence of the dii'ection and main channel, in which the thoughts and interests of men were then flowing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use particular facts not merely as isolated data but as symptomatic evidence that points to broader social or moral conditions; present facts as illustrative of trends or dispositions rather than ends in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prevalence and intensity of controversies as evidence of importance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The last point to which I shall appeal is the warmth and frequency of the religious controversies during the former of the two periods; the deep interest excited by them among all but the lowest and most ignorant classes; the importance attached to them by the very highest; the number, and in many instances, creditable merit, of the controversial publications..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue for the significance of a phenomenon by showing how often and how passionately it engages different social strata; cite quantity, social spread, and quality of engagement as corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge opposing views while persisting in critique
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have as little disposition as motive to recant the principles... Mute I still concede to the arguments for the present scheme of things as adduced in the preceding paragraph: but I likewise see, and always have seen, much that needs winnowing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate fair-mindedness by conceding plausible arguments from the other side, then explain why the main critique still stands; use measured language to strengthen credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ vivid, concrete anecdotes to evoke sympathy and ground abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Long illustrative anecdotes (e.g., the widow of Fort Augustus describing depopulated hamlets; the Laird raising a company and returning with maimed men who are then turned out of farms) are used to humanize and concretize the abstract social consequences discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor abstract claims in specific, emotionally resonant stories and testimonies from ordinary people to make moral and social harms palpable to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure argument by clear enumeration of ends or aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay enumerates the State's aims: "1. To make the means of existence more easy to each individual. 2. To secure to each of its members the hopes of bettering his own condition... 3. The development of those faculties which are essential to his humanity..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numbered lists or explicit headings to clarify the goals or premises that underlie the argument; this aids reader comprehension and rhetorical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer precise, descriptive paraphrase over vague universal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: "Instead of the position that all things find, it would be less equivocal and far more descriptive of the fact to say that things are always finding their level."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sweeping, abstract formulations; recast claims into more accurate, time-sensitive, or process-oriented phrasings that better describe observed reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative and historical examples to support generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: References to historical instances (the Roman character during the Triumvirate and under Tiberius, the reign of Charles II, Paris at the present moment) are invoked to show parallel moral consequences following revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolster present claims by drawing apt historical analogies or precedents that illustrate recurring patterns or outcomes; ensure comparisons are relevant and explicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose social systems by linking institutional practices to moral outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly connects systemic features (paper currency, national debt, overbalance of commercial spirit, enlargement of farms, poor laws) to moral and social consequences (pauperism, depopulation, degradation of character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing institutions, map concrete institutional mechanisms to their human effects; show causal pathways rather than asserting abstract harms without mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the reader's conscience with suppositional moral questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical moves such as asking the reader to recollect or imagine (e.g., "I must again entreat my reader to recollect..."; "Do you think, sir, that God allows of such proceedings?") are used to engage moral reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrogate the reader directly with moral hypotheticals and recollective prompts to provoke ethical engagement and self-questioning, increasing persuasive pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate ends appropriate to differing spheres (trade vs. agriculture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that "agriculture requires principles essentially different from those of trade" and that a gentleman should not view his estate as a merchant views stock; emphasizes different final causes and duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making normative recommendations, be attentive to the distinct logics and ends of different social spheres; tailor prescriptions to the institutional character and ultimate purposes of each sphere.
